explanations.answer: the lame and the blind and the mute
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The crowds come bringing "the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others," and they lay them at His feet. And Jesus heals them. Nobody on that mountain has to tiptoe up and hope He notices. They're set right down where He is.

Close, friend, but not this crowd. The Pharisees and the scribes show up earlier in the chapter, when they come to Jesus from Jerusalem (Matthew 15:1). On this mountain, the crowds bring "the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others." They lay them at His feet, and He heals them.

Not this time, friend. The text never mentions priests or elders on this mountain. The large crowds bring "the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others" and lay them at Jesus' feet. And He heals them.

True, baker! The crowd is amazed when they see "the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing." Then they glorify the God of Israel. That's a whole mountain of people with their jaws on the ground, and then their praise going up.

It's actually true, friend. The text says the crowd was amazed at the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. Then it says, "And they glorified the God of Israel." They saw it with their own eyes, and they praised Him for it.

Yes, baker, eat. Jesus says, "…they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat." Three days is a long stretch with an empty stomach. Jesus sees that, and He says it out loud to His disciples.

Nice try, friend, but clothes aren't the problem here. Jesus says the crowd has "nothing to eat." Three days with Him and no food. I've had a bad day or two, but I've never gone three days without a snack.

Not quite, baker. These people just watched the lame walk and the mute speak, so they've had plenty to do. What Jesus says is that they have "nothing to eat." He names the real need, and He names it first.

True, baker. Jesus says, "I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may faint along the way." He says it right after telling His disciples, "I have compassion for this crowd." He's already thinking about the road home.

It's true, friend. Jesus says, "I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may faint along the way." He is thinking about the walk home, and the disciples hear it straight from Him. Just before that He says, "I have compassion for this crowd."

explanations.answer: Where could we find enough bread out here
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The disciples ask, "Where in this desolate place could we find enough bread to feed such a large crowd?" They're looking at the empty land and the huge crowd. I'd have asked the same thing, and probably louder.

explanations.answer: Should we send them all home before dark
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. The disciples never bring up sending anyone home or the dark. They ask, "Where in this desolate place could we find enough bread to feed such a large crowd?" Jesus is the one who talks about not sending them away hungry.

explanations.answer: How much money do we have left to spend
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, because that's a very grown-up worry. But money never comes up in this passage. The disciples ask, "Where in this desolate place could we find enough bread to feed such a large crowd?" Their worry is where to find the bread.

Yes, baker! Matthew says, "And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground." Jesus tells a hungry crowd to sit before a single loaf has gone around. Whatever happens next, they get comfortable first.
Close, friend, but nobody is kneeling here. The text says Jesus "instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground." Sitting is what a crowd does when it's about to be served.
Not lying down, baker. I know three days is tiring, but the text says Jesus "instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground." Sitting it is.

That's right, baker. The text says, "Taking the seven loaves and the fish, He gave thanks and broke them." Seven loaves and a few small fish, and Jesus gives thanks. Thanks comes first, and then the breaking.
No, friend. Jesus doesn't send anyone for more. The text says, "Taking the seven loaves and the fish, He gave thanks and broke them." He works with what the disciples already brought Him.
Not that one, baker. Jesus never asks who is hungriest. He takes the seven loaves and the fish, and then "He gave thanks and broke them." Then He hands them to the disciples.
Careful, baker, this one is false. The text says, "They all ate and were satisfied." Everybody ate, and everybody was satisfied. Seven loaves and a few fish, and nobody got left out.
False is right, baker! Matthew says, "They all ate and were satisfied." That's all of them, not just some. Jesus said He didn't want to send them away hungry, and nobody went away hungry.

Yes, baker! Matthew says, "the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over." They all ate and were satisfied, and there was still more than they started with in loaves. Any baker would love that kind of leftovers.
Not quite, friend. Everyone ate until they were satisfied, and then "the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over." That's seven baskets of leftovers.

Good thinking, baker, but it's way more than that. The text says, "the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over." That's seven whole baskets after the whole crowd ate. The text doesn't say who got them.
That's right, baker. Matthew says, "After Jesus had dismissed the crowds, He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan." He came along the Sea of Galilee, so a boat fits right in.

explanations.answer: He rides off on a donkey
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. No donkey in this passage. The text says, "After Jesus had dismissed the crowds, He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan." A boat, not a donkey.
Not this time, baker. Jesus did go up on the mountain and sit down, but then He dismissed the crowds. After that, "He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan." He's on the move again.
